Abstract. This project trains and compares four neural network architectures for word-level language modeling: Dense Neural Network, LSTM, GRU, and Bidirectional LSTM. The models are trained on 2.6 million tokens from 18 classic English books from Project Gutenberg and evaluated using perplexity on a chronological 80/10/10 split. The GRU achieves the best validation perplexity of 503.9, which is 19.8 times better than random guessing and 1.69 times better than a unigram baseline. The main finding is that sequential processing matters more than parameter count — the Dense NN performs worst despite having the most parameters.

1. Introduction

A language model predicts the next word given the words before it. This is one of the core problems in NLP and forms the basis of tools like autocomplete and text generation.

This project builds four neural architectures and compares them on literary text. The main metric is perplexity (= exp(cross-entropy loss)). A perplexity of N means the model is as uncertain as picking from N equally likely words. Lower is better. Two baselines are used for context: a random baseline (perplexity = 10,000) and a unigram baseline (perplexity = 852.6, using word frequency with no context).

2. Dataset

The data is the NLTK Gutenberg corpus — 18 public-domain books that download automatically. It covers novels (Moby Dick, Emma), Shakespeare plays, the King James Bible, poetry, and other prose. The King James Bible alone is 1,010,654 tokens, about 38% of the whole corpus.

Word frequency follows Zipf's Law: a few words appear very often and most words are rare. The top 10 words are all function words: the, and, of, to, a, in, i, that, he, it.

3. Preprocessing

Three steps were applied to clean the raw text before training.

Lowercase

All words converted to lowercase so The and the count as the same word.

Punctuation removal

Only words passing word.isalpha() were kept. This removed 486,213 tokens (18.5%), leaving 2,135,400 clean tokens.

Vocabulary cutoff

The top 10,000 most frequent words were kept; everything else became <UNK>. These 10,000 words cover 96.21% of the corpus, so very little information is lost.

Sequence construction

A sliding window of length 20 with stride 3 built input-output pairs: 20 words in, predict the 21st. This produced 711,794 sequences total.

Train / Validation / Test split

Split chronologically (not randomly) to prevent the model from seeing future context during training.

4. Model Architectures

All four models take 20 word IDs as input, use an Embedding(10000, 64) layer, apply Dropout(0.3), and output probabilities over 10,000 words via Dense(10000, softmax). Loss: sparse categorical cross-entropy. Optimizer: Adam.

Model 1 — Dense Neural Network (2,290,832 parameters)

Flattens the 20 embeddings into one vector, then passes through Dense(256) and Dense(128) layers. Has no concept of word order. All position information is lost in the flatten step.

Model 2 — LSTM (2,028,816 parameters)

Reads words one at a time using three gates (forget, input, output) that control what the model remembers. Can capture dependencies between words far apart in the sequence.

Model 3 — GRU (2,004,496 parameters) — Best

A simpler version of LSTM with two gates (reset, update). About 25% fewer recurrent parameters than the LSTM. Converges faster and achieves lower perplexity on this dataset.

Model 4 — Bidirectional LSTM (1,996,048 parameters)

Two LSTMs run at the same time: one reads left-to-right, one reads right-to-left. Their outputs are combined into 128 dimensions. Despite the more complex setup, it underperforms the GRU on this task because looking at future words adds noise when the goal is to predict the next word.

Figure 5: Trainable parameter count for each of the four models.

5. Training

All models trained with the same settings. Early stopping monitored validation loss and stopped training if no improvement for 2 consecutive epochs, then restored the best weights. A fresh callback was created for each model to avoid shared state between runs.

7. Evaluation and Interpretation

Final test result

The test set was used once only, on the GRU after all model selection was done.

Table 6. GRU validation vs. test.

SplitPerplexityAccuracy
Validation503.912.30%
Test751.4112.01%

The test perplexity is higher than validation. This is expected, not a mistake. The split is chronological, so the test set is the last 10% of the corpus — the text furthest from what the model trained on. There is no data leakage.

Figure 11: GRU validation vs. test perplexity (left) and accuracy (right).

Top predicted words

The top-10 predicted next words were checked for three different seed phrases. The predictions shift depending on context: maritime words rise after a Moby Dick seed, biblical words rise after a Bible seed. This shows the model is doing real sequential reasoning, not just counting words.

Figure 12: Top-10 predicted next words for three seed phrases. Predictions change based on context.

Word embedding visualization

The GRU's 64-dimensional word embeddings were reduced to 2D using PCA. Words with similar meaning group together: maritime words (whale, sea, sailor) cluster in one area, religious terms in another, character names in their own spot. The model learned this structure just from predicting words.

Figure 13: PCA of the GRU's word embeddings. Semantic groups are visible: maritime, religious, and character name clusters.

8. Text Generation

Temperature controls how random the word choices are at each step. Low temperature = safe, repetitive. High temperature = more varied, less coherent.

  • Temperature 0.5: The model gets stuck repeating <UNK>. At low temperature the most likely word dominates every step, and since <UNK> is the most frequent token in the corpus it wins every time. This is a known issue with word-level models.
  • Temperature 0.8: Produces readable phrases with some unknowns. Mixes vocabulary from different books, reflecting the mixed training data.
  • Temperature 1.2: More varied words including biblical place names and maritime terms, but less grammatically coherent.

Figure 14: Generated text at three temperatures using the GRU model.

9. Analysis and Conclusion

Why GRU won

The GRU converges faster than the LSTM and reaches lower perplexity. Its two-gate design is simpler but works better for this corpus size. The Dense NN starts overfitting by epoch 2 while recurrent models continue improving.

Why Dense NN performed worst

Flattening the word embeddings throws away word order. The sequences "the dog bit the man" and "the man bit the dog" become identical inputs. With 2,290,832 parameters it has the most capacity but the worst result, which shows that architecture matters more than size for language modeling.

Why BiLSTM underperformed GRU

Predicting the next word should only use past words. The backward LSTM reads future words, which adds noise rather than useful information for this task. BiLSTM would likely outperform GRU on tasks like text classification where the full sentence is available.

Overfitting

Training perplexity drops to ~100–150 while validation stays around 500. The 18-book corpus is relatively small, so memorization happens quickly. Dropout and early stopping helped but did not fully solve the problem.

Key takeaways

  1. GRU > LSTM > BiLSTM > Dense NN on this corpus.
  2. Architecture matters more than parameter count for language modeling.
  3. Bidirectional context hurts when the task is inherently left-to-right.
  4. GRU is only 1.69× better than unigram — most predictability comes from word frequency, not context.
  5. Low temperature causes <UNK> loops in word-level models; subword tokenization would fix this.
  6. Word embeddings learn real semantic structure just from predicting the next word.

Possible improvements

  • Stacked LSTM or GRU layers for more capacity
  • Pre-trained embeddings (GloVe, Word2Vec)
  • Subword tokenization (BPE) to fix the <UNK> problem
  • Attention or transformer-based models
  • Larger training corpus
